analysis.one_liner: Extends federal authority to limit steel imports for another five years.
analysis.headline: A bill to extend steel import limits drew 249 House cosponsors — a bipartisan majority — but never left committee and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have extended the Steel Import Stabilization Act, a law that lets the President limit how much foreign steel can enter the United States, for five more years [S2] [S3]. Import limits tend to protect domestic steel mills and their workers, but they also raise the price of steel for the manufacturers and consumers who buy it. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Trade Subcommittee, which held hearings in the summer of 1989, but it was never voted on by the subcommittee, the full committee, or the House [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic steel producers and the steelworkers in steelmaking states, who would keep protection from foreign competition and, with it, steadier demand and prices for American-made steel. Steel-state communities depend heavily on mill jobs, so continued import limits shield those paychecks from foreign competition.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the Steel Import Stabilization Act — a law that gives the President power to restrict steel imports — for an additional five years, pushing its expiration from the fifth year to the tenth [S2] [S3].

Continued import limits keep foreign steel out of the market, supporting production levels and jobs at domestic steel mills, which are concentrated in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and other steelmaking states [S1] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Steel-using industries — automakers, appliance makers, construction firms — and, ultimately, consumers, who pay more for anything made with steel when imported steel is limited.

drawbacks.text: Import limits on steel raise the price of a basic industrial input, which flows through to the cost of cars, appliances, buildings, and other goods American families and businesses buy.
Shielding domestic mills from competition can reduce the pressure to modernize, leaving the industry less competitive over the long run — a cost steel state residents eventually bear themselves.
The bill simply extended an existing law for five more years without new conditions or reforms, locking in a protectionist arrangement as-is.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades higher steel prices for everyone who buys steel for steadier jobs in a small number of steelmaking communities. That protection is real and mattered to steel towns, but the costs are spread across every steel-using industry and consumer, and the bill offered no reforms to make the domestic industry stronger — just a straight five-year extension of existing import controls.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee and its Trade Subcommittee — which held four days of hearings in mid-1989 — but was never voted on, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. John Murtha introduced the bill on February 7, 1989, with 117 original cosponsors, and 249 members — 179 of 257 House Democrats and 70 of 175 House Republicans — signed on in total [S1] [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, then to the Subcommittee on Trade three days later [S5].
The Trade Subcommittee held hearings on four days between June 13 and August 1, 1989, but the bill was never reported out of subcommittee or committee and never reached the House floor [S5].
The bill expired with the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991, without any chamber voting on it [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died, steel-using manufacturers and consumers were spared five more years of import-driven steel price increases, while foreign steel exporters kept access to the U.S. market; domestic steel mills did not get the statutory extension they sought.

for.name: John Murtha
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized a large bipartisan list of original cosponsors from steel-producing districts.

for.name: 70 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making the support strongly bipartisan.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and committee leaders with control of the calendar
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Trade Subcommittee, held hearings, and never scheduled it for a subcommittee or full committee vote, keeping it off the House floor.

against.name: Steel-importing and steel-using interests
against.role: Manufacturers and importers who buy foreign steel
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending import limits, which raise the price and reduce the supply of imported steel they rely on.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily bipartisan: 179 of 257 House Democrats and 70 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored, so the bill's death in committee was not a party-line fight.

industries.note: Extended import limits would keep foreign steel out of the U.S. market, supporting domestic mills' sales and prices. Their gain comes directly at the expense of higher steel prices for manufacturers and consumers.
Extended import limits raise the cost and restrict the supply of a key industrial input, pushing up prices on goods these industries make and sell to the public.
The law underlying this bill lets the President restrict steel imports, so a five-year extension narrows foreign producers' access to the U.S. market.
